claim: Patients with Gorham-Stout disease (GSD) have lymphatic vessels in their bones.
source: Patients with Gorham-Stout disease (GSD) have lymphatic vessels in their bones and their bones gradually disappear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to published literature about GSD throughout the manuscript.

claim: Patients with Gorham-Stout disease (GSD) experience gradual bone disappearance.
source: Patients with Gorham-Stout disease (GSD) have lymphatic vessels in their bones and their bones gradually disappear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by historical case reports cited in the introduction.

claim: Mice that overexpress VEGF-C in bone exhibit a phenotype that resembles GSD.
source: Here, we report that mice that overexpress VEGF-C in bone exhibit a phenotype that resembles GSD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing bone lymphatics and bone loss in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice presented throughout the results section.

claim: Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc double-transgenic mice were generated to drive VEGF-C expression in bone.
source: To drive VEGF-C expression in bone, we generated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc double-transgenic mice.
evidence: This is described in the abstract and detailed in the methods and results sections.

claim: Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice developed lymphatics in their bones.
source: In contrast to Osx-tTA mice, Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice developed lymphatics in their bones.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessels in bones of Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.

claim: Inhibition of VEGFR3, but not VEGFR2, prevented the formation of bone lymphatics in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: We found that inhibition of VEGFR3, but not VEGFR2, prevented the formation of bone lymphatics in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that mF4-31C1 (VEGFR3 blocking antibody) prevented bone lymphatics while DC101 (VEGFR2 blocking antibody) had minimal effect.

claim: Bones from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were more porous than bones from Osx-tTA mice.
source: Radiological and histological analysis revealed that bones from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were more porous and had more osteoclasts than bones from Osx-tTA mice.
evidence: This is supported by μCT imaging data and histological analysis showing increased cortical bone porosity.

claim: Bones from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had more osteoclasts than bones from Osx-tTA mice.
source: Radiological and histological analysis revealed that bones from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were more porous and had more osteoclasts than bones from Osx-tTA mice.
evidence: This is supported by TRAP staining data showing significantly more osteoclasts per mm of bone in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.

claim: Bone loss in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice could be attenuated by an osteoclast inhibitor.
source: Importantly, we found that bone loss in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice could be attenuated by an osteoclast inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that zoledronic acid treatment reduced osteoclast numbers and cortical bone porosity.

claim: The mutant phenotype of Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice could be reversed by inhibiting the expression of VEGF-C.
source: We also discovered that the mutant phenotype of Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice could be reversed by inhibiting the expression of VEGF-C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that doxycycline treatment caused bone lymphatics to disappear and bone structure to normalize.

claim: Expression of VEGF-C in bone is sufficient to induce the pathologic hallmarks of GSD in mice.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that expression of VEGF-C in bone is sufficient to induce the pathologic hallmarks of GSD in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data showing bone lymphatics, bone loss, and chylothorax in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.

claim: Lymphatic vessels perform several essential functions in the body including absorbing intestinal lipids, transporting immune cells, and returning fluid and macromolecules to the blood vasculature.
source: Lymphatic vessels perform several essential functions in the body. Lymphatic vessels absorb intestinal lipids, transport immune cells, and return fluid and macromolecules to the blood vasculature (Witte et al., 1997; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most soft tissues in the body have lymphatic vessels.
source: Most soft tissues in the body have lymphatic vessels (Witte et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Hard tissues such as enamel, dentin, and bone do not have lymphatic vessels.
source: In contrast, hard tissues such as enamel, dentin, and bone do not have lymphatic vessels.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Gorham-Stout disease (GSD) is a sporadic disease characterized by the presence of lymphatics in bone and bone loss.
source: Gorham-Stout disease (GSD) is a sporadic disease that is characterized by the presence of lymphatics in bone and bone loss (Gorham and Stout, 1955; Dellinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature including the landmark Gorham and Stout paper.

claim: J.B.S. Jackson is credited with publishing the first case of GSD in 1838.
source: J.B.S. Jackson is credited with publishing the first case of GSD, which appeared in the Boston Medical and Surgical Journal in 1838 (Jackson, 1838).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jackson's 1838 publication.

claim: Jackson described a patient whose humerus had completely disappeared in his 1838 paper entitled 'A Boneless Arm'.
source: In his paper entitled 'A Boneless Arm', Jackson described a patient whose humerus had completely disappeared (Jackson, 1838).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jackson's 1838 publication.

claim: Gorham and colleagues published a paper describing two additional cases of massive bone loss.
source: Over 100 years later, Gorham and colleagues published a paper that described two additional cases of massive bone loss (Gorham et al., 1954).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gorham et al., 1954.

claim: Gorham and colleagues found that bones from one patient were filled with irregular vessels.
source: They were able to analyze multiple affected bones from one patient and found that the bones were filled with irregular vessels (Gorham et al., 1954).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gorham et al., 1954.

claim: Gorham and Stout acquired biopsy specimens from seven patients and observed abnormal vessels in each specimen.
source: Over several years, Gorham and Stout were able to acquire biopsy specimens from seven patients seen by other physicians (Gorham and Stout, 1955). They observed abnormal vessels in each of the bone biopsy specimens they analyzed (Gorham and Stout, 1955).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gorham and Stout, 1955.

claim: Gorham and Stout reported that massive bone loss is associated with the growth of vessels in bone.
source: This finding led Gorham and Stout to report that massive bone loss is associated with the growth of vessels in bone (Gorham and Stout, 1955).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gorham and Stout, 1955.

claim: Bones from GSD patients are filled with lymphatic vessels.
source: It is now known that bones from GSD patients are filled with lymphatic vessels (Lala et al., 2013; Ozeki et al., 2016; Edwards et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent publications.

claim: More than 300 cases of GSD have been described since Gorham and Stout's landmark publication.
source: Since Gorham and Stout's landmark publication, more than 300 cases of GSD have been described (Dellinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: GSD affects males and females equally.
source: GSD affects males and females equally and is most commonly diagnosed in children and young adults (Dellinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: GSD is most commonly diagnosed in children and young adults.
source: GSD affects males and females equally and is most commonly diagnosed in children and young adults (Dellinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The course of GSD is often unpredictable.
source: The course of this disease is often unpredictable.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about GSD.

claim: In some GSD patients, the disease progresses slowly over years, while in others it progresses rapidly over months.
source: In some patients, the disease progresses slowly over a period of years, whereas in others, it progresses rapidly over a period of months (Dellinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In severe GSD cases, the disease progresses until entire bones are lost and replaced by fibrous tissue.
source: In severe cases, the disease progresses until entire bones are lost and replaced by fibrous tissue.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about GSD.

claim: GSD is reported to arrest and stabilize after a variable period of activity.
source: The disease is reported to arrest and stabilize after a variable period of activity.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about GSD.

claim: Affected bones do not regenerate after GSD has arrested.
source: Importantly, affected bones do not regenerate after the disease has arrested (Dellinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: GSD can affect any bone in the body but most frequently affects the ribs and vertebrae.
source: Although GSD can affect any bone in the body, it most frequently affects the ribs and vertebrae (Dellinger et al., 2014; Lala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Thoracic involvement in GSD is associated with a poor prognosis.
source: Unfortunately, thoracic involvement is associated with a poor prognosis because these patients tend to develop chylothorax, a complication that can cause respiratory distress, failure, and death (Lala et al., 2013; Ludwig et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GSD patients with thoracic involvement tend to develop chylothorax.
source: Unfortunately, thoracic involvement is associated with a poor prognosis because these patients tend to develop chylothorax, a complication that can cause respiratory distress, failure, and death (Lala et al., 2013; Ludwig et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Chylothorax can cause respiratory distress, failure, and death.
source: Unfortunately, thoracic involvement is associated with a poor prognosis because these patients tend to develop chylothorax, a complication that can cause respiratory distress, failure, and death (Lala et al., 2013; Ludwig et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The cause of GSD remains unknown.
source: Despite advances in the understanding of the clinical features of the disease, the cause of GSD remains unknown and there are no standard treatments for this disease.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about GSD.

claim: There are no standard treatments for GSD.
source: Despite advances in the understanding of the clinical features of the disease, the cause of GSD remains unknown and there are no standard treatments for this disease.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about GSD.

claim: VEGF-C is the principle driver of lymphangiogenesis.
source: Vascular endothelial growth factor-C (VEGF-C) is the principle driver of lymphangiogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Full-length VEGF-C undergoes proteolytic processing, which increases its affinity for VEGFR2 and VEGFR3.
source: Full-length VEGF-C undergoes proteolytic processing, which increases its affinity for VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 (Joukov et al., 1996; Joukov et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of VEGF-C impairs the development of the lymphatic vasculature.
source: Studies with genetically engineered mice have revealed that loss of VEGF-C impairs the development of the lymphatic vasculature.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies with genetically engineered mice.

claim: Mice that completely lack VEGF-C do not form lymphatics.
source: Mice that completely lack VEGF-C do not form lymphatics, whereas mice that lack a single copy of the VEGF-C gene develop fewer lymphatics than wildtype mice (Dellinger et al., 2007; Karkkainen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Mice that lack a single copy of the VEGF-C gene develop fewer lymphatics than wildtype mice.
source: Mice that completely lack VEGF-C do not form lymphatics, whereas mice that lack a single copy of the VEGF-C gene develop fewer lymphatics than wildtype mice (Dellinger et al., 2007; Karkkainen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Tissue-specific overexpression of VEGF-C has been shown to induce lymphangiogenesis in the pancreas.
source: Conversely, tissue-specific overexpression of VEGF-C has been shown to induce lymphangiogenesis in the pancreas (Mandriota et al., 2001), lungs (Yao et al., 2014), and skin (Jeltsch et al., 1997; Lohela et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Tissue-specific overexpression of VEGF-C has been shown to induce lymphangiogenesis in the lungs.
source: Conversely, tissue-specific overexpression of VEGF-C has been shown to induce lymphangiogenesis in the pancreas (Mandriota et al., 2001), lungs (Yao et al., 2014), and skin (Jeltsch et al., 1997; Lohela et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Tissue-specific overexpression of VEGF-C has been shown to induce lymphangiogenesis in the skin.
source: Conversely, tissue-specific overexpression of VEGF-C has been shown to induce lymphangiogenesis in the pancreas (Mandriota et al., 2001), lungs (Yao et al., 2014), and skin (Jeltsch et al., 1997; Lohela et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Osterix (Osx) is a transcription factor expressed by chondrocytes, osteocytes, and osteoblasts.
source: Osterix (Osx) is a transcription factor expressed by chondrocytes, osteocytes, and osteoblasts (Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A transgenic mouse line was previously created in which the expression of a tetracycline transactivator (tTA) cassette was placed under the control of the Osx promoter.
source: A transgenic mouse line was previously created in which the expression of a tetracycline transactivator (tTA) cassette was placed under the control of the Osx promoter (Rodda and McMahon, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the publication describing the mouse line.

claim: The Osx-tTA transgenic mouse line has a TetO-Cre::GFP cassette located immediately downstream of the tTA cassette.
source: This transgenic mouse line also has a TetO-Cre::GFP cassette located immediately downstream of the tTA cassette (Rodda and McMahon, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the publication describing the mouse line.

claim: GFP was expressed by chondrocytes, osteocytes, and osteoblasts in Osx-tTA-TetO-Cre::GFP mice.
source: GFP was expressed by chondrocytes, osteocytes, and osteoblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP was not expressed by cells in the kidney, liver, lung, pancreas, skeletal muscle, or spleen in Osx-tTA-TetO-Cre::GFP mice.
source: GFP was not expressed by cells in the kidney, liver, lung, pancreas, skeletal muscle, or spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: tTA activity in Osx-tTA-TetO-Cre::GFP mice is restricted to bone.
source: These data show that tTA activity in Osx-tTA-TetO-Cre::GFP mice (herein referred to as Osx-tTA) is restricted to bone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GFP expression pattern data.

claim: No viable Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc offspring were obtained from crosses between Osx-tTA and TetO-Vegfc mice without doxycycline suppression.
source: No viable Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc offspring were obtained from these crosses.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were grossly indistinguishable from control littermates on E12.5.
source: Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were grossly indistinguishable from control littermates on E12.5.
evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were severely edematous and displayed enlarged lymphatics on E14.5.
source: However, Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were severely edematous and displayed enlarged lymphatics on E14.5.
evidence: This is supported by images and histology shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were in the process of being resorbed on E16.5.
source: All Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were in the process of being resorbed on E16.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: VEGF-C expression by bone cells during embryonic development has a lethal effect.
source: These data indicate that VEGF-C expression by bone cells during embryonic development has a lethal effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc embryos die by E16.5.

claim: Lymphatic vessels were not present in femurs from 21, 28, or 35-day-old Osx-tTA mice.
source: Lymphatic vessels were not present in femurs from 21, 28, or 35-day-old Osx-tTA mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lymphatic vessels were not present in femurs from 21-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: Similarly, lymphatic vessels were not present in femurs from 21-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lymphatic vessels were present in femurs from 28-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: In contrast, lymphatic vessels were present in femurs from 28-day-old Ox-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lymphatic vessels in 28-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were restricted to cortical bone.
source: However, lymphatic vessels were restricted to cortical bone (the dense outer shell of bone).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice, lymphatic vessels were located in cortical bone, trabecular bone, and the marrow cavity.
source: In 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice, lymphatic vessels were located in cortical bone, trabecular bone, and the marrow cavity (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Tibias and ribs from 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had lymphatics.
source: Tibias and ribs from 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice also had lymphatics (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lymphatic vessels in bones of Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice expressed Lyve-1.
source: These vessels expressed Lyve-1, another marker of lymphatic endothelium (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had hyperplastic lymphatics in bones.
source: Although 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had hyperplastic lymphatics in bones, lymphatics in soft tissues (kidney, liver, lungs, and pancreas) appeared normal and the circulating level of VEGF-C was not elevated (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1 and 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lymphatics in soft tissues (kidney, liver, lungs, and pancreas) appeared normal in 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: Although 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had hyperplastic lymphatics in bones, lymphatics in soft tissues (kidney, liver, lungs, and pancreas) appeared normal and the circulating level of VEGF-C was not elevated (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The circulating level of VEGF-C was not elevated in 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: Although 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had hyperplastic lymphatics in bones, lymphatics in soft tissues (kidney, liver, lungs, and pancreas) appeared normal and the circulating level of VEGF-C was not elevated (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Expression of VEGF-C in bone induces the formation of bone lymphatics, but not the growth of lymphatics in distant tissues.
source: These data indicate that expression of VEGF-C in bone induces the formation of bone lymphatics, but not the growth of lymphatics in distant tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that bone lymphatics are hyperplastic while soft tissue lymphatics appear normal.

claim: VEGF-C activates VEGFR2 and VEGFR3.
source: VEGF-C activates VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 (Joukov et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: VEGF-C is thought to primarily induce lymphangiogenesis by activating VEGFR3.
source: However, VEGF-C is thought to primarily induce lymphangiogenesis by activating VEGFR3 (Veikkola et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The density of bone lymphatics was modestly reduced in DC101-treated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: The density of bone lymphatics was modestly reduced in DC101-treated mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Bone lymphatics failed to form in mF4-31C1-treated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: In contrast, bone lymphatics failed to form in mF4-31C1-treated mice (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: VEGFR3 signaling is required for the development of bone lymphatics in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: These data show that VEGFR3 signaling is required for the development of bone lymphatics in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that mF4-31C1 (VEGFR3 blocking antibody) prevented bone lymphatic formation.

claim: Murine VEGF-D only activates VEGFR3.
source: In contrast to murine VEGF-C, murine VEGF-D only activates VEGFR3 (Baldwin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A transgenic mouse strain was recently created in which the expression of murine VEGF-D is controlled by doxycycline.
source: A transgenic mouse strain was recently created in which the expression of murine VEGF-D is controlled by doxycycline (Lammoglia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Femurs from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfd mice were filled with lymphatic vessels.
source: Importantly, femurs from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfd mice were filled with lymphatic vessels (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Activation of VEGFR3 is sufficient for the formation of bone lymphatics.
source: These data show that activation of VEGFR3 is sufficient for the formation of bone lymphatics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that VEGF-D (which only activates VEGFR3) induces bone lymphatics.

claim: Femurs from 21-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice appeared normal and were indistinguishable from femurs from Osx-tTA mice.
source: Femurs from 21-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice appeared normal and were indistinguishable from femurs from Osx-tTA mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Femurs from 28- and 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had a moth-eaten appearance.
source: In contrast, femurs from 28- and 35-day-old Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had a moth-eaten appearance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The development of the moth-eaten bone phenotype coincided with the formation of lymphatics in cortical bone.
source: The development of this phenotype coincided with the formation of lymphatics in cortical bone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the timing of lymphatic formation (P28) with the appearance of the moth-eaten phenotype (P28).

claim: Bones from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were significantly more porous than bones from Osx-tTA mice.
source: This revealed that bones from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were significantly more porous than bones from Osx-tTA mice (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by μCT imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Femurs from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were significantly weaker than femurs from Osx-tTA mice.
source: The three-point bending assay revealed that femurs from Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were significantly weaker than femurs from Osx-tTA mice (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by three-point bending assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lymphatic endothelial cells do not directly degrade bone.
source: After culturing cells for 72 hr, we observed numerous resorption pits in wells containing differentiated RAW264.7 cells (osteoclasts), but not in wells containing LECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). This finding suggests that LECs do not directly degrade bone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the osteo-assay plate experiment showing LECs do not create resorption pits.

claim: Osteoclasts are multi-nucleated cells that degrade bone and display tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) activity.
source: Osteoclasts are multi-nucleated cells that degrade bone and display tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about osteoclasts.

claim: There were significantly more osteoclasts on the surface of cortical bone in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice than in Osx-tTA mice.
source: This staining revealed that there were significantly more osteoclasts on the surface of cortical bone in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice than in Osx-tTA mice (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by TRAP staining and quantitative data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CTX-1 is a small peptide generated by osteoclast-mediated cleavage of collagen I.
source: CTX-1 is a small peptide generated by osteoclast-mediated cleavage of collagen I (Garnero et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: CTX-1 was significantly higher in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice than Osx-tTA mice.
source: Importantly, CTX-1 was significantly higher in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice than Osx-tTA mice (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The number and activity of osteoclasts are increased in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: Together, these data show that the number and activity of osteoclasts are increased in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from TRAP staining and CTX-1 data.

claim: Zoledronic acid is a drug that accumulates in bone and prevents bone resorption by inhibiting farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase activity in osteoclasts.
source: Zoledronic acid (also known as Zometa) is a drug that accumulates in bone and prevents bone resorption by inhibiting farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase activity in osteoclasts (Clézardin, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The density of bone lymphatics was not significantly different between zoledronic acid-treated and vehicle-treated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: The density of bone lymphatics was not significantly different between zoledronic acid-treated and vehicle-treated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The number of osteoclasts was significantly lower in zoledronic acid-treated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice than vehicle-treated mice.
source: However, the number of osteoclasts and porosity of femurs were significantly lower in zoledronic acid-treated mice than vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by TRAP staining and quantitative data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The porosity of femurs was significantly lower in zoledronic acid-treated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice than vehicle-treated mice.
source: However, the number of osteoclasts and porosity of femurs were significantly lower in zoledronic acid-treated mice than vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and quantitative data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Bone loss in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice is driven by osteoclasts.
source: These data indicate that bone loss in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice is driven by osteoclasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that zoledronic acid (an osteoclast inhibitor) reduces bone loss.

claim: Femurs from mF4-31C1-treated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had significantly fewer osteoclasts than femurs from vehicle-treated mice.
source: We found that femurs from mF4-31C1-treated mice had significantly fewer osteoclasts than femurs from vehicle-treated mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by TRAP staining and quantitative data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Femurs from mF4-31C1-treated Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice were significantly less porous than femurs from vehicle-treated mice.
source: Additionally, we found that femurs from mF4-31C1-treated mice were significantly less porous than femurs from vehicle-treated mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and quantitative data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Inhibition of lymphangiogenesis can prevent osteoclastogenesis and bone loss in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
source: These data show that inhibition of lymphangiogenesis can prevent osteoclastogenesis and bone loss in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that mF4-31C1 treatment prevents both bone lymphatics and bone loss.

claim: VEGF-C mRNA levels were approximately 350-fold higher in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice than Osx-tTA mice.
source: VEGF-C mRNA levels were approximately 350-fold higher in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice than Osx-tTA mice.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: VEGF-C mRNA levels in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice returned to normal within 3 days of being placed back on doxycycline water.
source: Importantly, VEGF-C mRNA levels in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice returned to normal within 3 days of being placed back on doxycycline water (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Doxycycline rapidly inhibits the expression of VEGF-C in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice.

claim: Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice that received normal water from E18.5 to P35 had an expanded network of lymphatics in their periosseous muscle.

claim: Ribs in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice had a moth-eaten appearance.

claim: Doxycycline caused cortical bone porosity in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice to revert back to normal.

claim: The circulating levels of CTX-1 in Osx-tTA;TetO-Vegfc mice returned to normal after exposure to doxycycline.
